01_Thermal_energy_and_reaction_surroundi.title: Thermal energy and reaction surroundings
01_Thermal_energy_and_reaction_surroundi.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Identify a reaction as exothermic or endothermic from the direction of thermal energy transfer and the resulting temperature change of the surroundings.
Distinguish the reacting chemicals (the system) from everything else being observed (the surroundings), and identify the surroundings' temperature as the quantity that is actually measured.

prerequisites.statement: Particles with more kinetic energy are, on average, at a higher temperature; when a substance transfers thermal energy to its surroundings, the surroundings' temperature rises, and when it takes thermal energy from them, their temperature falls.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Classifying a reaction depends on linking a measured temperature change to a direction of energy transfer, not just reading a number off a thermometer.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate a change by subtracting an initial reading from a final reading, keeping the sign of the result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The entire classification tool used in this lesson is the sign of $\Delta T = T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}$.

prerequisites.statement: Read a thermometer scale to the nearest labelled or half-labelled division and record the value with its unit, $^\circ$C.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A correct classification is only as reliable as the two readings it is built from.

diagnostic_items.question: A beaker of liquid reads $15.0\,^\circ$C before a solid dissolves in it. Two minutes later it reads $9.0\,^\circ$C. Calculate $\Delta T$, showing the sign.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner subtracts the smaller reading from the larger one instead of final minus initial, losing the sign that carries the direction of transfer.
The subtraction is correct in size, but dropping the sign throws away the one piece of information the rest of the lesson depends on.
The learner reports the final reading alone instead of the change between the two readings.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks signed subtraction before any chemistry is attached to it: get the arithmetic secure first, then attach meaning to the sign.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write final reading and initial reading as two separate numbers, subtract in that fixed order (final $-$ initial), and check the sign makes sense: a falling reading must give a negative result.

theory_blocks.title: What you measure is never the reaction itself
theory_blocks.body:
You cannot put a thermometer directly 'into' a chemical change and read off its energy. What you can do is put a thermometer into everything *around* the reaction — the water it is dissolved in,

the air in the test tube, the metal of a calorimeter — and watch how that surrounding material's temperature changes.

Chemists call the reacting chemicals the [[blue:**system**]] and everything else being observed — the solvent, the container, the air, the thermometer itself — the **surroundings**.

A reaction transfers thermal energy between the system and the surroundings. The direction of that transfer is exactly what the surroundings' temperature change reveals: warmer surroundings mean energy has moved *out* of the system,

cooler surroundings mean energy has moved *in*.

theory_blocks.title: Exothermic and endothermic, defined by direction
theory_blocks.body:
An **exothermic** reaction transfers thermal energy *to* its surroundings. The reaction mixture and its immediate surroundings typically become warmer, so a thermometer placed in the surroundings reads a *higher* value after the reaction than before.

An **endothermic** reaction transfers thermal energy *from* its surroundings into the reacting system. The surroundings typically become cooler, so the thermometer reads a *lower* value after the reaction than before.

Both directions are measured the same way: record the surroundings' temperature before mixing ($T_{\text{initial}}$) and again once the change is clearly underway or complete ($T_{\text{final}}$), then calculate

$$\Delta T = T_{\text{final}} - T_{\text{initial}}.$$

$\Delta T>0$ (a rise) signals exothermic; $\Delta T<0$ (a fall) signals endothermic. The sign of $\Delta T$ is the classification — no other reading is needed.

assets.caption: Thermometer readings for two insulated cups, both starting at $20\,^\circ$C. Left: an exothermic reaction raises the surroundings to $27\,^\circ$C ($\Delta T=+7\,^\circ$C), transferring energy out. Right: an endothermic reaction lowers the surroundings to $13\,^\circ$C ($\Delta T=-7\,^\circ$C), taking energy in.
assets.purpose: Make the link between a physical thermometer reading, the sign of $\Delta T$ and the direction of energy transfer concrete and simultaneous, for both cases side by side.

theory_blocks.title: A fixed procedure for classifying any reaction
theory_blocks.body:
1. Record the surroundings' temperature just before mixing: $T_{\text{initial}}$.
2. Record the surroundings' temperature once the change is underway (or at a fixed, stated time): $T_{\text{final}}$.
3. Calculate $\Delta T = T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}$, keeping the sign.
4. If $\Delta T>0$, the reaction is exothermic. If $\Delta T<0$, the reaction is endothermic.

This procedure works regardless of what the starting temperature happened to be, because step 3 removes the starting value from the final answer: only the *change* survives.

theory_blocks.title: Needing a push to start is not the same as the overall direction
theory_blocks.body:
Some reactions need an initial nudge — a spark, a flame, some gentle warming — before they get going at all. That starting help is not what exothermic or endothermic describes.

[[blue:Classification is read from what the surroundings' temperature does once the reaction is actually proceeding]], by the four-step procedure above, never from how the reaction was started.

theory_blocks.title: Everyday exothermic and endothermic changes
theory_blocks.body:
A reusable hand warmer that is clicked or shaken and becomes hot is exothermic: it transfers thermal energy to your hands.

A first-aid instant cold pack that is squeezed and becomes cold is endothermic: it takes thermal energy from the injury it is placed against.

Both are judged exactly the same way as any laboratory example: compare a temperature reading before and after.

keywords.definition: The reacting chemicals in a reaction being studied.
Everything around the reacting chemicals that can be observed or measured, such as the solvent, the container and the thermometer.
Describes a reaction that transfers thermal energy to its surroundings, raising their temperature.
Describes a reaction that takes thermal energy from its surroundings, lowering their temperature.
The signed temperature change of the surroundings, calculated as final reading minus initial reading.

worked_examples.statement: **A reaction in an insulated cup.** A mixture in an insulated cup starts at $20\,^\circ$C. Two minutes after mixing it reads $27\,^\circ$C. Classify the reaction.
reasoning: Calculate the signed temperature change, final minus initial.
Compare the sign of $\Delta T$ to the rule: positive means exothermic, negative means endothermic.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta T = 27-20=+7\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Since $\Delta T>0$, the surroundings warmed up, so the reaction is **exothermic**: it transferred thermal energy out to the surrounding liquid.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $20+7=27$, matching the final reading, so the subtraction is consistent.

worked_examples.statement: **A solid dissolving.** A different solid is stirred into water in an insulated cup starting at $20\,^\circ$C. The reading falls steadily to $13\,^\circ$C as it dissolves. Classify this process and state the direction of energy transfer.
reasoning: Calculate $\Delta T$ in the same fixed order, final minus initial.
A negative $\Delta T$ means the surroundings cooled, so energy must have moved into the dissolving solid from the water.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta T = 13-20=-7\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Since $\Delta T<0$, the process is **endothermic**: thermal energy was taken from the surrounding water, cooling it.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing this as 'releasing cold' rather than 'absorbing thermal energy'. Cold is not a substance that is released; the water simply loses thermal energy to the dissolving solid.

worked_examples.statement: **Two experiments, different starting points.** Group A's mixture starts at $18\,^\circ$C and ends at $25\,^\circ$C. Group B's mixture starts at $30\,^\circ$C and ends at $29\,^\circ$C. Group B's final reading is higher than Group A's initial reading. Does that make Group B's reaction more exothermic? Classify both.
reasoning: Absolute temperature readings cannot be compared across two different experiments; only each experiment's own $\Delta T$ is meaningful.
Calculate $\Delta T$ for Group A and for Group B separately, in the same fixed order.
worked_examples.solution: Group A: $\Delta T = 25-18=+7\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, exothermic. Group B: $\Delta T = 29-30=-1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, endothermic — even though $29\,^\circ$C is numerically higher than $18\,^\circ$C.
worked_examples.interpretation:
Group B's surroundings actually cooled slightly during its reaction, so it is endothermic, despite ending at a higher absolute temperature than Group A started.

Classification never compares one experiment's reading to another's; it compares each experiment's own before-and-after readings.

worked_examples.statement: **Evaluate a classmate's reasoning.** A student mixes two chemicals in a polystyrene cup starting at $21\,^\circ$C; after 3 minutes it reads $34\,^\circ$C. The student writes: 'This must be exothermic because the chemicals obviously started cold and ended up hot, so heat was obviously made.' Evaluate this reasoning and give the correct scientific justification.
unknowns: Whether the conclusion is right, and the correct justification
reasoning: Separate the conclusion (exothermic) from the reasoning used to reach it ('started cold, ended hot').
The correct justification is never about how the reactants 'felt' — it is the calculated sign of $\Delta T$.
worked_examples.solution:
The student's conclusion is correct, but the reasoning is not scientifically valid. First, $21\,^\circ$C is not 'cold': words like 'cold' and 'hot' are impressions, not evidence.

Second, heat is not 'made': energy cannot be created, only transferred. The correct justification is: $\Delta T = 34-21=+13\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a positive value, so the surroundings gained thermal energy, and that energy was transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings.

This transfer of thermal energy to the surroundings is what makes the reaction exothermic.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using vague temperature impressions ('felt cold', 'felt hot') instead of the calculated, signed $\Delta T$ as the justification — exactly the error behind the misconception that exothermic reactions must start from hot reactants.

worked_examples.statement: **A new context: reusable heat packs and cold packs.** A reusable heat pack rises from $18\,^\circ$C to $42\,^\circ$C when activated. A first-aid cold pack falls from $21\,^\circ$C to $4\,^\circ$C when activated. Classify each pack and state the direction of energy transfer between the pack and the skin it is placed against.
reasoning: Treat each pack as its own experiment and apply the four-step procedure.
Link the sign of $\Delta T$ to the direction of transfer between the pack (surroundings, from the chemical reaction's point of view) and the skin.
worked_examples.solution:
Heat pack: $\Delta T=42-18=+24\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, exothermic; the reaction inside transfers thermal energy outward, warming the skin it touches. Cold pack: $\Delta T=4-21=-17\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, endothermic;

the reaction inside takes thermal energy from its surroundings, including the skin it touches, cooling it.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same four-step classification rule used for a laboratory cup applies unchanged to a commercial product: only the sign of $\Delta T$ matters.

guided_exercises.statement: A reaction mixture in an insulated cup is recorded at $24.0\,^\circ$C before mixing and $31.0\,^\circ$C two minutes after. Calculate $\Delta T$ and classify the reaction, stating the direction of energy transfer.
hints: Identify which reading is $T_{\text{initial}}$ and which is $T_{\text{final}}$.
Match the sign of $\Delta T$ to exothermic (positive) or endothermic (negative).
guided_exercises.answer: $\Delta T=31.0-24.0=+7.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; exothermic, energy transferred out to the surroundings.
common_errors: Subtracting in the wrong order (initial minus final), which flips the sign and the classification.

guided_exercises.statement: A student records: 'I mixed vinegar and the solid in a cup. The cup, the vinegar and the thermometer all got colder.' Identify the chemical system and the surroundings in this description, then state what the falling temperature tells you about the direction of energy transfer.
hints: The system is whichever substances are actually reacting with each other.
The surroundings are everything the thermometer could be sitting in or touching that is not itself reacting.
A falling surroundings' temperature means energy has moved from the surroundings into the system.
guided_exercises.answer: System: the reacting chemicals, which are the acid in the vinegar and the solid. Surroundings: the water in the vinegar, the cup and the thermometer. The falling temperature shows thermal energy moving from the surroundings into the reacting system, so the reaction is endothermic.
common_errors: Treating the cup or the thermometer as part of the 'reaction' rather than as surroundings being used to observe it.

exercises.statement: A reaction's surroundings are recorded at $16.0\,^\circ$C before mixing and $22.5\,^\circ$C after. Calculate $\Delta T$ and classify the reaction.
exercises.full_solution: Final minus initial: $22.5-16.0=6.5$, a positive value, so energy was transferred to the surroundings.

exercises.statement: A student investigates a reaction between a metal and an acid in a polystyrene cup. Identify the system and the surroundings in this set-up, and explain which one the thermometer actually measures.
exercises.answer: System: the metal and the acid. Surroundings: the cup, any excess solution not reacting, and the thermometer itself. The thermometer measures the surroundings, not the system directly.

exercises.statement: A classmate says: 'Endothermic reactions let off heat — that's why the cup feels warm while it happens.' Explain what is wrong with this statement and rewrite it correctly.
exercises.answer: The statement is wrong on both the direction and the observed effect: an endothermic reaction takes thermal energy in from the surroundings, so the cup should feel cooler, not warmer. Corrected: endothermic reactions take thermal energy from their surroundings, so the surrounding cup and liquid become colder.
common_errors: Confusing 'endo-' (into the system) with 'exo-' (out of the system).

exercises.statement: A sports injury spray is applied to skin and the skin's surface temperature falls from $32\,^\circ$C to $24\,^\circ$C within seconds. Using the same reasoning you used for laboratory cups, classify the change that happens as the spray acts on the skin and explain your answer in terms of the direction of energy transfer.
exercises.answer: $\Delta T=24-32=-8\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; endothermic. The change in the spray (the liquid evaporating on the skin) takes thermal energy from the skin (its surroundings), lowering the skin's temperature.
exercises.full_solution: The spray is simply a different context for the same four-step procedure: identify before/after surroundings temperature, subtract in the fixed order, and read the sign.

exam_questions.statement: A student records the temperature of the surroundings of a reaction as $17.0\,^\circ$C before mixing and $29.0\,^\circ$C after. (a) Calculate $\Delta T$. (b) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. (c) Explain, in terms of energy transfer, why the surroundings' temperature changed in this direction.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\Delta T=29.0-17.0=+12.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (b) Exothermic. (c) The positive $\Delta T$ shows the surroundings gained thermal energy; this energy was transferred out of the reacting chemicals (the system) into the surroundings during the reaction.
mark_scheme: Correct signed subtraction: $29.0-17.0=+12.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
Correctly identifies exothermic from the positive sign.
States that thermal energy was transferred from the system to the surroundings.
Links the rise in surroundings' temperature directly to that transfer.

exam_questions.statement: Describe a method, using a thermometer and an insulated cup, to determine whether dissolving a solid in water is exothermic or endothermic. Your answer should include what is measured, when it is measured, and how the result is used to classify the process.
exam_questions.answer: Place a measured volume of water in an insulated cup and record its temperature before adding the solid ($T_{\text{initial}}$). Add the solid, stir to help it dissolve, and record the temperature again once it has dissolved or after a fixed time ($T_{\text{final}}$). Calculate $\Delta T=T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}$. If $\Delta T$ is positive, the process is exothermic; if $\Delta T$ is negative, it is endothermic.
mark_scheme: Uses an insulated cup to reduce unwanted energy exchange with the room.
Records a temperature before adding the solid.
Records a temperature again after dissolving, at a clear, consistent point.
Calculates $\Delta T$ as final minus initial.
States the correct rule linking the sign of $\Delta T$ to exothermic/endothermic.

mcq.stem: A reaction mixture is already warm, at $40\,^\circ$C, before two chemicals are combined in it. After mixing, the surroundings' temperature falls to $35\,^\circ$C. How should this reaction be classified?

options.text: Endothermic, because $\Delta T=35-40=-5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is negative.
Exothermic, because the mixture started hot.
options.why_wrong: the starting temperature is irrelevant to the classification; only the change in temperature, here a fall, decides it.

options.text: Exothermic, because $40\,^\circ$C is a high starting temperature.
options.why_wrong: a high starting temperature says nothing about the direction of the change; the mixture’s temperature still fell, which is the endothermic signature.

options.text: There is not enough information to classify it.
options.why_wrong: there is enough information: the before and after temperatures are both given, so $\Delta T$ can be calculated directly.

mcq.explanation: $\Delta T=35-40=-5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a fall, so the reaction is endothermic. The starting temperature being high is irrelevant: only the sign of the change decides the classification.

mcq.stem: Which statement about an endothermic reaction is correct?

options.text: It releases thermal energy to its surroundings, which warm up.
options.why_wrong: this describes an exothermic reaction; an endothermic reaction takes energy in, so the surroundings cool rather than warm.

options.text: It takes thermal energy from its surroundings, which cool down.
It always needs a flame to start and keep going.
options.why_wrong: needing a flame to start is about activation energy, a separate idea from whether the overall reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

options.text: It has no effect on the surroundings' temperature.
options.why_wrong: the surroundings’ temperature does change: it falls, because thermal energy is being taken from them.

mcq.explanation: 'Endo-' means into the system: an endothermic reaction takes thermal energy from its surroundings, so the surroundings' temperature falls.

mcq.stem: In an experiment where a solid dissolves in water inside a cup, what exactly does the thermometer measure?

options.text: The temperature of the chemical bonds inside the solid directly.
options.why_wrong: a thermometer cannot be placed inside the solid’s bonds; it only ever measures the surrounding water.

options.text: The total energy released or absorbed by the reaction, in joules.
options.why_wrong: a thermometer reads temperature in °C, not an energy value in joules; the energy change has to be calculated separately from the temperature data.

options.text: The surrounding water's temperature, used as evidence for the direction of energy transfer.
The rate at which the solid is dissolving.
options.why_wrong: temperature and rate of dissolving are different quantities; a thermometer gives no direct reading of how fast the solid is dissolving.

mcq.explanation: A thermometer can only be placed in the surroundings (here, the water), never inside the reacting system itself; its reading is used as evidence of energy transfer, not a direct measurement of the system.

mcq.stem: Two experiments are recorded. Experiment 1: $22\,^\circ$C before, $25\,^\circ$C after. Experiment 2: $22\,^\circ$C before, $19\,^\circ$C after. A student says both experiments are 'the same' because they both start at $22\,^\circ$C. What is the correct way to report the two experiments?

options.text: Both exothermic, since they start at the same temperature.
options.why_wrong: the two experiments have different final temperatures (25°C and 19°C), so they cannot both be exothermic; only experiment 1 actually warms up.

options.text: Both endothermic, since both involve a change from $22\,^\circ$C.
options.why_wrong: experiment 1’s temperature rises, which is the exothermic signature, not endothermic; a matching starting temperature does not make both changes the same type.

options.text: They cannot be compared because they have different final readings.
options.why_wrong: different final readings are exactly what let the two experiments be compared and classified separately, not a reason to avoid comparing them.

options.text: Experiment 1 is exothermic ($\Delta T=+3\,^\circ$C); experiment 2 is endothermic ($\Delta T=-3\,^\circ$C).

mcq.explanation: Matching starting temperatures tell you nothing about classification; only each experiment's own $\Delta T$ does. $\Delta T_1=25-22=+3\,^\circ$C (exothermic); $\Delta T_2=19-22=-3\,^\circ$C (endothermic).

flashcards.back: A reaction that transfers thermal energy to its surroundings, so the surroundings' temperature rises ($\Delta T>0$).
A reaction that takes thermal energy from its surroundings, so the surroundings' temperature falls ($\Delta T<0$).

flashcards.front: True or false: an endothermic reaction releases heat, making its container feel warm.
flashcards.back: False. Endothermic means the reaction takes thermal energy in from its surroundings, so the container feels cooler, not warmer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the 'system' and the 'surroundings' in a reaction?
flashcards.back: The system is the reacting chemicals themselves. The surroundings are everything else being observed — the solvent, the container, the thermometer — which is what you actually measure.

flashcards.front: How do you classify a reaction from two thermometer readings?
flashcards.back: Calculate $\Delta T = T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}$. $\Delta T>0$: exothermic. $\Delta T<0$: endothermic.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A reaction is exothermic only if the reacting chemicals themselves already feel hot before you start mixing them.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday use of 'hot' and 'cold' describes how something feels right now, so learners default to judging the starting materials rather than tracking a change.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner classifies from the starting temperature of the reactants, or refuses to classify a reaction that starts cold even when it then warms up.
misconceptions.correct_model: Exothermic describes what the reaction does: it transfers thermal energy to its surroundings as it proceeds, so the surroundings' temperature rises, whatever temperature the reactants started at.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two reactions that both start at the same temperature but one warms the surroundings and one does not; only the change matters.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An endothermic reaction releases heat, which is why the container can feel warm while it happens.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word 'reaction' is associated with things happening and releasing energy (fizzing, glowing, exploding), so learners attach 'releases energy' to every reaction by default.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says an endothermic reaction 'gives off heat' or predicts a temperature rise for a reaction already labelled endothermic.
misconceptions.correct_model: An endothermic reaction takes thermal energy from its surroundings, so the surroundings' temperature falls. 'Endo-' means into the reacting system, not out of it.
misconceptions.remediation: Physically handle an endothermic example (an instant cold pack or a solid dissolving in water that cools the cup) and record the falling reading directly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Whatever the final temperature reads is the answer that should be reported, without comparing it to where the reading started.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A single final number looks like a complete result, and the starting reading is easy to treat as just a setup step rather than data to keep.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reports only the final reading, or classifies two experiments as 'the same' because they end at similar final temperatures despite very different starting points.
misconceptions.correct_model: Classification never comes from one reading alone. It comes from $\Delta T = T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}$: a rise ($\Delta T>0$) signals exothermic, a fall ($\Delta T<0$) signals endothermic.
misconceptions.remediation: Give two experiments with different starting temperatures but the same final temperature and ask which, if either, is exothermic; only $\Delta T$ decides it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Classifying a reaction from how hot or cold the reactants feel before mixing.
common_mistakes.why: This confuses the starting condition with the direction of transfer during the reaction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always calculate $\Delta T$ from two readings of the surroundings, before and after, and read the sign.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying an endothermic reaction 'releases heat' or 'releases cold'.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday language treats 'cold' as something that can be given off, which has no physical meaning here.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Describe endothermic changes as 'taking thermal energy from the surroundings', never as 'releasing cold'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting only the final temperature as the result of an experiment.
common_mistakes.why: A single reading cannot show direction of change; it could be high or low for many unrelated reasons.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always report both readings and the calculated, signed $\Delta T$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Subtracting the two readings in the wrong order.
common_mistakes.why: Reversing the order flips the sign of $\Delta T$ and gives the opposite classification.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Fix the order every time: final reading minus initial reading.

exam_notes: State $\Delta T$ with its sign explicitly before giving the classification — examiners look for the working, not just the final word 'exothermic' or 'endothermic'.
When asked to describe a method, always include both temperature readings and when each is taken, not just 'use a thermometer'.
Never justify a classification using how the reactants 'felt' before mixing; justify it using the calculated $\Delta T$.
If a question gives two experiments, compare each one's own $\Delta T$ separately — never compare one experiment's final reading to another experiment's initial reading.

summary.big_idea: Exothermic and endothermic describe the direction of thermal energy transfer between a reaction and its surroundings, and that direction is read entirely from the sign of the surroundings' temperature change.
key_points: The system is the reacting chemicals; the surroundings are what a thermometer actually measures.
Calculate $\Delta T = T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}$, always in that order, keeping the sign.
$\Delta T>0$: exothermic, energy transferred to the surroundings.
$\Delta T<0$: endothermic, energy taken from the surroundings.
The starting temperature of the reactants, and how the reaction was started, do not decide the classification — only $\Delta T$ does.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Classification always comes from the sign of $\Delta T$, never from a single reading or from how the reactants felt before mixing.
