02_Reaction_pathways_H_and_activation_en.title: Reaction pathways, ΔH and activation energy
02_Reaction_pathways_H_and_activation_en.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Interpret a reaction pathway diagram showing an exothermic or an endothermic reaction, by comparing the energy level of the products with the energy level of the reactants.
Interpret a labelled reaction pathway diagram to state the sign and size of $\Delta H$ and the size of the activation energy $E_a$.

Construct and label a scaled reaction pathway diagram for a stated exothermic or endothermic case, positioning the reactant level, the product level and the activation-energy peak correctly relative to one another.

prerequisites.statement: Read a value from a labelled axis and from a horizontal reference line on a graph.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every quantity in a pathway diagram (reactant level, product level, peak) is read as a height against the vertical energy axis.

prerequisites.statement: Classify a reaction as exothermic or endothermic from the sign of its surroundings' temperature change.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: $\Delta H$'s sign in a pathway diagram must agree with the exothermic/endothermic classification already met in an earlier lesson: negative $\Delta H$ matches exothermic, positive $\Delta H$ matches endothermic.

prerequisites.statement: Subtract two numerical values and keep the sign of the result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: $\Delta H$ and $E_a$ are both calculated as one energy level minus another.

theory_blocks.title: Up or down: classifying a reaction from the two levels
theory_blocks.body:
A **reaction pathway diagram** plots energy up the vertical axis against reaction progress along the horizontal axis. The reactants are drawn as a flat level on the left, the products as a flat level on the right, and a curve joins the two.

To classify the reaction you only have to compare those two flat levels:

- [[green:Products drawn below the reactants]] — the chemicals end up storing less energy, so energy has been transferred out to the surroundings. The reaction is **exothermic**, and the temperature of the surroundings rises, exactly as in an earlier lesson.
- [[red:Products drawn above the reactants]] — the chemicals end up storing more energy, so energy has been taken in from the surroundings. The reaction is **endothermic**, and the temperature of the surroundings falls.

Nothing else on the diagram changes this answer: the height of the hump in between does not affect it, and no numbers are needed — which of the two flat levels is drawn higher is enough.

assets.caption: Two reaction pathway diagrams. Left: the products are drawn below the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic. Right: the products are drawn above the reactants, so the reaction is endothermic.
assets.purpose: Lets a Core student classify a reaction from a pathway diagram by comparing the two flat levels alone, with no $\Delta H$ or $E_a$ labelling.

theory_blocks.title: A hill, not a cliff
theory_blocks.body:
Imagine rolling a ball from a starting point, over a hill, down to a resting point that is lower than where it started. Overall, the ball ends up lower — it has 'released' height.

But to get there, it still had to be pushed up and over the top of the hill first, even though the far side is lower than the start.

A reaction pathway works the same way. A reaction can [[green:release energy overall]] (its products end up at a lower energy than its reactants) and still require an initial [[orange:'push' over a barrier]] before that release can happen.

The overall drop and the height of the barrier are two separate features of the same hill — one does not determine the other.

theory_blocks.title: $\Delta H$: the overall energy difference
theory_blocks.body:
A reaction pathway diagram plots energy (vertical axis) against reaction progress (horizontal axis — *not* time). The reactants are drawn as a flat level on the left; the products are drawn as a flat level on the right.

$$\Delta H = E_{\text{products}} - E_{\text{reactants}}.$$

If the products are drawn below the reactants, $E_{\text{products}}<E_{\text{reactants}}$, so $\Delta H<0$: exothermic, matching a rise in surroundings' temperature as in an earlier lesson.

If the products are drawn above the reactants, $\Delta H>0$: endothermic, matching a fall in surroundings' temperature.

In an exam the energy axis is normally scaled in kJ/mol, so $\Delta H$ is quoted in kJ/mol as well. The arithmetic is identical whatever unit the axis carries.

theory_blocks.title: $E_a$: the barrier measured from the reactants
theory_blocks.body:
The pathway between reactants and products is not flat: it rises to a peak before falling (or continuing to fall) to the product level.

This peak represents the point at which old bonds are part-broken and new bonds are part-formed — the least stable, highest-energy arrangement along the whole pathway.

The **activation energy**, $E_a$, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react. On the diagram, it is read as the rise *from the reactant level up to the peak*:

$$E_a = E_{\text{peak}} - E_{\text{reactants}}.$$

$E_a$ is always measured from the reactant level, never from the product level, and it is always a positive height — the peak is always drawn above the reactants, whichever way the overall reaction goes.

assets.caption: An exothermic pathway: reactants at 100 units, products at 60 units ($\Delta H=60-100=-40$ units), peak at 150 units ($E_a=150-100=50$ units, measured from the reactants).
assets.purpose: Shows a fully labelled, numerically scaled exothermic pathway with $\Delta H$ and $E_a$ drawn as two distinct arrows from their correct reference levels.

theory_blocks.title: Drawing a labelled pathway diagram, step by step
theory_blocks.body:
1. Draw and label the axes: energy (vertical), reaction progress (horizontal, not time).
2. Draw a flat horizontal reactant level, starting from the vertical axis.
3. Decide the case: for an exothermic reaction, draw the product level *below* the reactant level; for an endothermic reaction, draw it *above*.
4. Join reactants to products with a smooth curve that rises to a single peak *above both* levels, then falls to the product level.
5. Draw the $E_a$ arrow from the reactant level straight up to the peak — never starting from the product level.
6. Draw the $\Delta H$ arrow between the reactant level and the product level, and label it with its sign.
7. Label both arrows with their calculated values.

The two most common labelling faults are starting the $E_a$ arrow from the product level instead of the reactant level, and drawing the peak level with the products instead of above both levels — both break the definitions in steps 5 and 4.

assets.caption: The opposite case, endothermic: reactants at 60 units, products at 100 units ($\Delta H=100-60=+40$ units), peak at 130 units ($E_a=130-60=70$ units, still measured from the reactants, not the products).
assets.purpose: Shows the construction rule applied to the opposite case, with the product level now above the reactants and $E_a$ still correctly anchored to the reactant level.

theory_blocks.title: Reading the axis correctly
theory_blocks.body:
The horizontal axis shows how far the reaction has progressed from reactants to products, not elapsed time: it cannot be used to say how fast or slow the reaction is.

And because $E_a$ is always measured from the reactant level, a reaction can have [[orange:a large $E_a$ (slow to get started)]] and still be [[blue:strongly exothermic overall (a large negative $\Delta H$)]] — these are two independent features of the same diagram,

as the earlier hill analogy showed.

keywords.definition: A diagram plotting energy against reaction progress, showing the reactant level, the product level and the peak between them.
The overall energy change of a reaction, calculated as the energy of the products minus the energy of the reactants.
The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur, measured as the rise from the reactant level to the peak of the pathway.
The horizontal axis of a pathway diagram, showing how far the reaction has advanced from reactants to products; it is not a measure of time.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading $\Delta H$ from a diagram.** A labelled pathway diagram shows reactants at 100 energy units and products at 60 energy units. Calculate $\Delta H$ and state the sign.
reasoning: $\Delta H$ is always products minus reactants, in that order.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta H = 60-100=-40$ units. Negative, so this is an exothermic pathway.
worked_examples.interpretation: A negative $\Delta H$ confirms the products end up lower on the diagram than the reactants, consistent with energy having been transferred out to the surroundings.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading $E_a$ from the same diagram.** Using the same diagram (reactants at 100 units, peak at 150 units), calculate the activation energy $E_a$.
reasoning: $E_a$ is measured from the reactant level up to the peak, never from the product level.
worked_examples.interpretation: Notice $E_a=50$ units is a completely different number from $\Delta H=-40$ units calculated in the previous example, even though both come from the same diagram — they are measured between different pairs of levels.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calculating $150-60=90$ (peak minus products) instead of $150-100$ (peak minus reactants) treats $E_a$ as if it were measured from the wrong level.

worked_examples.statement: **The opposite case.** A second pathway diagram shows reactants at 60 units, products at 100 units, and a peak at 130 units. Calculate $\Delta H$ and $E_a$, and explain why $E_a$ is still measured from the reactant level even though the reactants are now the *lower* of the two flat levels.
reasoning: Apply the same two definitions as before: $\Delta H$ from products and reactants, $E_a$ from the peak and the reactants, regardless of which level happens to be higher.
The *definition* of $E_a$ never changes: it is always the barrier that must be crossed starting from wherever the reaction begins, which is always the reactant level.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta H=100-60=+40$ units: positive, endothermic, matching the products sitting above the reactants. $E_a=130-60=70$ units, still measured from the reactant level up to the peak.
worked_examples.interpretation: This directly contradicts the idea that $\Delta H$ is positive 'when products are lower': here the products are higher and $\Delta H$ is positive, which is the correct pattern.

worked_examples.statement: **Full interpretation.** An unfamiliar pathway diagram shows reactants at 80 units, products at 50 units and a peak at 120 units. (a) State $\Delta H$ with its sign and explain your reasoning. (b) State $E_a$. (c) Explain why this reaction still needs an input of energy to start, even though it is exothermic overall.
reasoning: (a) $\Delta H=E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$.
(b) $E_a=E_{\text{peak}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$.
(c) Link the existence of the peak to the need for an initial input of energy, independent of the sign of $\Delta H$.

worked_examples.statement: **From numbers to a sketch.** Without being given a drawn diagram, you are told: reactants are at 200 units, the activation energy is 60 units, and $\Delta H=-150$ units. State the energy level of the peak and of the products, and describe in words how the diagram should be sketched.
reasoning: Rearrange $E_a=E_{\text{peak}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$ to find the peak level.
Rearrange $\Delta H=E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$ to find the product level.
worked_examples.solution:
$E_{\text{peak}}=200+60=260$ units. $E_{\text{products}}=200+(-150)=50$ units. The diagram should show a flat reactant level at 200, rising to a peak at 260,

then falling well below the reactant level to a flat product level at 50, since the negative $\Delta H$ means a strongly exothermic reaction.
worked_examples.interpretation: This example works the construction rule backwards: starting from the two defining relationships rather than from a ready-made picture, which is exactly what is needed to draw a diagram from scratch.

guided_exercises.statement: A pathway diagram shows reactants at 90 units, products at 55 units and a peak at 140 units. Calculate $\Delta H$ and $E_a$.
hints: $E_a$ compares the peak to the reactants, not the products.
Check that $E_a$ comes out positive; it always should.
common_errors: Calculating $E_a$ as peak minus products ($140-55=85$) instead of peak minus reactants.

guided_exercises.statement: A reaction is endothermic with reactants at 50 units and $\Delta H=+25$ units, and has an activation energy of 45 units. Find the energy level of the products and of the peak, then describe how you would sketch and label the diagram.
hints: Rearrange $\Delta H=E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$ to find the product level.
Rearrange $E_a=E_{\text{peak}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$ to find the peak level.
The peak must end up above both the reactant and the product level.
guided_exercises.answer: Products: $50+25=75$ units. Peak: $50+45=95$ units. Sketch: flat reactant line at 50, rising through a peak at 95, falling to a flat product line at 75 (above the reactants, since the reaction is endothermic), with the $E_a$ arrow drawn from 50 up to 95 and the $\Delta H$ arrow drawn from 50 up to 75.
common_errors: Drawing the peak below the product level, which is never possible since the peak is always the highest point on the whole pathway.

exercises.statement: A pathway diagram shows reactants at 120 units, products at 90 units and a peak at 155 units. Calculate $\Delta H$ and $E_a$, and state the classification.
A student drew a pathway diagram and started the $E_a$ arrow at the product level instead of the reactant level. Explain why this is incorrect, and state what the $E_a$ arrow should actually show.
exercises.answer: $E_a$ is defined as the barrier a reaction must cross starting from the reactants, since that is where every reaction begins; it has nothing to do with where the products end up. The arrow should run from the reactant level straight up to the peak, not from the product level.

exercises.statement: Explain why an exothermic reaction can still have a large activation energy, using the hill analogy from this lesson.
exercises.answer: An exothermic reaction's products end up at a lower overall energy than its reactants, but the pathway between them can still rise to a high peak first — like a ball that must be pushed over a tall hill even though it then rolls down to a point lower than where it started. The size of the drop ($\Delta H$) and the height of the climb ($E_a$) are independent features of the same pathway.

exercises.statement: A reaction has reactants at 180 energy units, an activation energy of 75 units and $\Delta H=-120$ units. Find the energy at the top of the activation barrier and the products' energy level.
exercises.full_solution: The peak is $180+75=255$ units. Since $\Delta H=E_{products}-E_{reactants}=-120$, $E_{products}=180-120=60$ units.

exercises.statement: A reaction pathway diagram is drawn with the product level above the reactant level. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and state what happens to the temperature of the surroundings.
exercises.answer: Endothermic: the products store more energy than the reactants, so energy has been taken in from the surroundings and the temperature of the surroundings falls.

exam_questions.statement: A pathway diagram shows reactants at 130 kJ/mol, products at 170 kJ/mol and a peak at 195 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate $\Delta H$, with its sign. (b) State the classification. (c) Calculate $E_a$.
mark_scheme: Correct subtraction for $\Delta H$: $170-130=+40$ kJ/mol.
Correct sign interpreted as endothermic.
Correct subtraction for $E_a$: $195-130=65$ kJ/mol, from the reactant level.

exam_questions.statement: Describe how you would draw and label a fully correct pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, given numerical values for the reactant level, the product level and the peak level. Your answer should explain where each arrow starts and ends.
exam_questions.answer: Draw labelled axes (energy vertical, reaction progress horizontal). Draw a flat reactant level and, below it, a flat product level, since the reaction is exothermic. Join them with a smooth curve rising to a single peak above both levels, then falling to the product level. Draw the $E_a$ arrow from the reactant level straight up to the peak. Draw the $\Delta H$ arrow between the reactant level and the product level, labelled with a negative sign. Label every level with its numerical value.
mark_scheme: Both axes present and correctly labelled (energy; reaction progress, not time).
Product level correctly drawn below the reactant level for an exothermic case.
Curve rises to a single peak above both flat levels.
$E_a$ arrow correctly starts at the reactant level and ends at the peak.
$\Delta H$ arrow correctly drawn between reactant and product levels, with the negative sign stated.
All three levels labelled with their numerical values.

exam_questions.statement:
The reaction pathway diagram below is for a reaction. The energy axis is scaled in kJ/mol.

(a) Name the feature labelled **W** and the feature labelled **X**. [2]

(b) Name the quantity shown by arrow **Y** and the quantity shown by arrow **Z**. [2]

(c) Use the values on the energy axis to calculate $E_a$ and $\Delta H$ for this reaction. Give the unit, and give a sign for $\Delta H$. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) **W** is the energy level of the reactants; **X** is the energy level of the products. (b) **Y** is the activation energy, $E_a$; **Z** is the overall energy change of the reaction, $\Delta H$. (c) $E_a=550-400=150$ kJ/mol. $\Delta H=280-400=-120$ kJ/mol; the negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic.
mark_scheme: **W** identified as the reactants (their energy level).
**X** identified as the products (their energy level).
**Y** identified as the activation energy, $E_a$.
**Z** identified as the overall energy change of the reaction, $\Delta H$.
$E_a=550-400=150$ kJ/mol, with the unit given.
$\Delta H=280-400=-120$ kJ/mol, with the negative sign given.

assets.caption: Reaction pathway diagram for part (a) to part (c): the energy axis is marked at 280, 400 and 550 kJ/mol, and the labels W, X, Y and Z have to be named.
assets.purpose: Gives students a drawn, kJ/mol-scaled pathway diagram to read and label, as Cambridge C5.1.6 questions do.

challenge_questions.statement: Reaction X has $\Delta H=-25$ units and $E_a=15$ units, both measured from a reactant level of 110 units. Reaction Y has the same $\Delta H=-25$ units and the same reactant level of 110 units, but $E_a=40$ units. (a) Calculate the product level and the peak level for each reaction. (b) Although X and Y release exactly the same overall energy, explain one practical difference you would expect between them.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Both reactions: products $=110-25=85$ units. X: peak $=110+15=125$ units. Y: peak $=110+40=150$ units. (b) X has a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of colliding particles will have enough energy to react at a given temperature; X would be expected to proceed faster than Y under the same conditions, even though both release the same overall energy once they do react.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The two reactions share $\Delta H$ and therefore share the overall energy release and the product level, but they differ entirely in $E_a$, which is an independent feature of the pathway controlling how hard it is to start the reaction, not how much energy it eventually releases.

mcq.stem: A pathway diagram shows reactants at 70 kJ/mol, products at 40 kJ/mol and a peak at 110 kJ/mol. What are $\Delta H$ and $E_a$?

options.text: $\Delta H=-30$ kJ/mol, $E_a=40$ kJ/mol.
$\Delta H=40$ kJ/mol and $E_a=40$ kJ/mol (the same number).
options.why_wrong: $\Delta H$ should be the signed drop from reactants to products ($40-70=-30$), not the raw products value, and it should not equal $E_a$ by coincidence.

options.text: $\Delta H=-30$ kJ/mol, $E_a=70$ kJ/mol.
options.why_wrong: $E_a$ is measured from the reactant level to the peak ($110-70=40$), not from the peak down to zero or to another level; using 70 here mixes up the levels.

options.text: $\Delta H=-70$ kJ/mol, $E_a=30$ kJ/mol.
options.why_wrong: $-70$ is just the reactant level with a minus sign, not products minus reactants ($40-70=-30$); and $30$ is the size of $\Delta H$, not the rise from the reactants to the peak ($110-70=40$).

mcq.explanation: $\Delta H=40-70=-30$ kJ/mol. $E_a=110-70=40$ kJ/mol. The two numbers are different because they are measured from different pairs of levels.

mcq.stem: Which statement about activation energy is correct?

options.text: Exothermic reactions do not need any activation energy, since they release energy overall.
options.why_wrong: every reaction pathway, exothermic or endothermic, still rises to a peak above the reactants before it can proceed; releasing energy overall does not remove that barrier.

options.text: Every reaction, whether exothermic or endothermic, must cross an energy barrier above the reactant level.
Activation energy is only relevant for endothermic reactions.
options.why_wrong: activation energy applies to every reaction pathway, not only to endothermic ones; it is about the barrier to reaction, separate from the overall energy change.

options.text: Activation energy equals $\Delta H$ whenever the reaction is exothermic.
options.why_wrong: $E_a$ and $\Delta H$ are measured between different pairs of levels (reactants-to-peak versus reactants-to-products), so they are generally different numbers even for exothermic reactions.

mcq.explanation: The existence of a peak above the reactant level applies to every reaction pathway; whether the overall reaction releases or absorbs energy is a separate question about where the products end up.

mcq.stem: A pathway diagram shows the product level drawn above the reactant level. What does this tell you about $\Delta H$?

options.text: $\Delta H$ is negative, so the reaction is exothermic.
options.why_wrong: a higher product level means more energy stored in the products than the reactants, which is the endothermic case, not exothermic.

options.text: $\Delta H$ cannot be determined without knowing the peak height.
options.why_wrong: $\Delta H$ only compares the reactant and product levels; the peak height affects $E_a$, not $\Delta H$, so it can be found without it.

options.text: $\Delta H$ is positive, so the reaction is endothermic.
$\Delta H$ is zero, since the diagram still shows a complete pathway.
options.why_wrong: $\Delta H$ is zero only if the product and reactant levels are equal; here the products are drawn clearly above the reactants, so $\Delta H$ is not zero.

mcq.explanation: $\Delta H=E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$; if products are drawn higher than reactants, this subtraction is positive, which is the endothermic case, independent of the peak height.

mcq.stem: Which description of the activation-energy arrow on a correctly drawn pathway diagram is right?

options.text: It starts at the product level and ends at the peak.
options.why_wrong: starting from the product level instead of the reactant level measures the wrong quantity; $E_a$ is defined from the reactants’ own starting level.

options.text: It starts at the reactant level and ends at the product level.
options.why_wrong: an arrow from the reactant level straight to the product level represents $\Delta H$, not $E_a$; it skips over the peak entirely.

options.text: It starts at the peak and ends at the product level.
options.why_wrong: this arrow runs in the wrong direction and from the wrong level; $E_a$ rises up to the peak starting from the reactants, not down from the peak.

options.text: It starts at the reactant level and ends at the peak.

mcq.explanation: $E_a$ is always the rise from the reactant level up to the peak; starting it anywhere else, such as from the product level, measures a different (and usually meaningless) quantity.

mcq.stem: A reaction pathway diagram shows the products drawn at a lower energy level than the reactants. What does the diagram tell you about the reaction?

options.text: It is exothermic: energy is transferred out to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It is endothermic: energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
options.why_wrong: products drawn lower means the chemicals end up storing less energy than they started with, so energy has been transferred out — that is the exothermic case, not the endothermic one.

options.text: It is exothermic, but only if the peak is also drawn below the reactant level.
options.why_wrong: the peak is always drawn above the reactant level on every pathway diagram; the classification depends only on the product level compared with the reactant level.

options.text: Nothing can be decided until the energy levels are given as numbers.
options.why_wrong: the classification follows from which of the two flat levels is drawn higher, so numerical values are not needed for it.

mcq.explanation: Products drawn below the reactants means the chemicals end up storing less energy, so energy has been transferred out to the surroundings: the reaction is exothermic and the surroundings warm up, matching an earlier lesson.

flashcards.front: What is $\Delta H$ on a reaction pathway diagram?
flashcards.back: The overall energy difference between products and reactants: $\Delta H=E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$.
The minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen, read as the rise from the reactant level up to the peak: $E_a=E_{\text{peak}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$.

flashcards.front: True or false: an exothermic reaction does not need any activation energy.
flashcards.back: False. Every reaction pathway rises to a peak above the reactants first; an exothermic reaction can still have a large $E_a$ even though it releases energy overall.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between $\Delta H$ and $E_a$?
flashcards.back: $\Delta H$ compares products to reactants (the overall change). $E_a$ compares the peak to the reactants only (the barrier to get started). They are measured from different pairs of levels and are usually different numbers.

flashcards.front: How do you find the peak level if you know the reactant level and $E_a$?

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The activation energy $E_a$ is the same quantity as $\Delta H$, just read differently.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both quantities are read off the same diagram as vertical distances, so learners conflate two different vertical measurements into one.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner gives the same numerical value for $E_a$ and $\Delta H$, or uses the peak-to-product distance when asked for $E_a$.
misconceptions.correct_model: $\Delta H$ is the overall difference between products and reactants (where the pathway ends up compared to where it started). $E_a$ is the height of the barrier above the reactants that must be climbed before any product can form. They are measured from different reference points and are generally different numbers.
misconceptions.remediation: Work through one diagram calculating both quantities side by side, each time stating which two levels are being subtracted.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An exothermic reaction does not need any activation energy, because it releases energy overall.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners assume that an overall energy release means nothing has to be 'paid' to get the reaction going.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws an exothermic pathway with no peak, or states that $E_a$ is zero or does not apply for exothermic reactions.
misconceptions.correct_model: Every reaction, exothermic or endothermic, must pass over an energy barrier (the peak) before products can form. An exothermic reaction can release a large amount of overall energy and still have a large $E_a$ — the two are independent.
misconceptions.remediation: Use the rolling-ball-over-a-hill analogy: the ball must still be pushed over the top of the hill even if the far side is much lower than the start.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: $\Delta H$ is positive when the products are drawn lower than the reactants.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes reverse the 'higher means more energy' convention, or focus on which side of the diagram looks 'bigger' rather than on actual vertical position.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner labels a diagram where products sit below reactants as endothermic, or vice versa.
misconceptions.correct_model: $\Delta H = E_{\text{products}} - E_{\text{reactants}}$. Products drawn *lower* than reactants give a negative $\Delta H$ (exothermic). Products drawn *higher* than reactants give a positive $\Delta H$ (endothermic).
misconceptions.remediation: Always calculate $\Delta H$ numerically from the two labelled levels rather than judging it from the picture alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Measuring $E_a$ from the product level instead of the reactant level.
common_mistakes.why: The peak-to-product distance looks like a similarly sized vertical gap on the diagram, so it is easy to grab by mistake.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always state the two levels being subtracted before calculating: $E_a$ is always peak minus reactants.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming an exothermic reaction has no activation energy.
common_mistakes.why: An overall energy release is wrongly taken to mean nothing needs to be 'paid' to start the reaction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember the hill analogy: every pathway still climbs to a peak above the reactants before any product can form.

common_mistakes.mistake: Judging the sign of $\Delta H$ from the picture alone instead of calculating it.
common_mistakes.why: Diagrams are sometimes drawn with product and reactant levels close together, making the direction hard to judge by eye.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always calculate $E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$ numerically rather than estimating from the drawing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the horizontal axis as a measure of time.
common_mistakes.why: Most other graphs met in GCSE science plot a quantity against time, so the habit carries over.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that the horizontal axis is reaction progress, and that the diagram says nothing about how fast the reaction is.

exam_notes: When asked for $\Delta H$ or $E_a$, always state the subtraction explicitly (e.g. $150-100$) before giving the final value — examiners credit the method, not just the number.
Always state which level an arrow starts and ends at when describing a pathway diagram; 'the gap' is not precise enough.
Remember $E_a$ is always measured from the reactant level, whichever way the overall reaction goes.
The horizontal axis label should read 'reaction progress' (or equivalent), never 'time'.
Energy levels in Cambridge pathway diagrams are given in kJ/mol — always write the unit after your value for $\Delta H$ or $E_a$, and keep the minus sign on $\Delta H$ for an exothermic reaction.

summary.big_idea: A reaction pathway diagram separates two independent quantities: $\Delta H$, the overall energy difference between products and reactants, and $E_a$, the energy barrier that must always be crossed from the reactants first.
key_points: $\Delta H=E_{\text{products}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$: negative is exothermic, positive is endothermic.
$E_a=E_{\text{peak}}-E_{\text{reactants}}$, always measured from the reactant level.
The peak is always drawn above both the reactant and the product level, whichever way the reaction goes.
An exothermic reaction can still have a large $E_a$ — the overall drop and the initial climb are independent.
The horizontal axis is reaction progress, not time.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: $\Delta H$ and $E_a$ are measured from different pairs of levels and are almost always different numbers — never assume they are equal.

03_Why_bond_changes_can_heat_or_cool.jso.title: Why bond changes can heat or cool
03_Why_bond_changes_can_heat_or_cool.jso.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: State that breaking chemical bonds always requires an input of energy and that forming new chemical bonds always releases energy.
Explain, from the relative sizes of the energy absorbed breaking bonds and the energy released forming bonds, whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall.

prerequisites.statement: A reaction's overall direction is exothermic if it transfers energy out overall (negative $\Delta H$) and endothermic if it takes energy in overall (positive $\Delta H$), from an earlier lesson.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson explains *why* a reaction ends up exothermic or endothermic, by looking inside the pathway at what bond breaking and bond making each contribute.

prerequisites.statement: A chemical bond is a strong attraction holding atoms together; separating two bonded atoms requires energy to overcome that attraction.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This is the physical reason breaking any bond always costs energy, which this lesson builds on directly.

prerequisites.statement: Compare two numbers and state which is larger and by how much.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The overall direction of a reaction is found by comparing the total energy absorbed breaking bonds with the total energy released forming bonds.

theory_blocks.title: Pulling magnets apart, letting them click together
theory_blocks.body:
Two magnets stuck together are attracted to each other, similarly to how two bonded atoms are held together by a chemical bond.

Pulling those two magnets apart takes a deliberate pull from you — you have to put energy in to overcome the attraction.

Letting two separate magnets come together and click, on the other hand, needs no push from you at all: they release energy themselves (you can feel the snap) as they settle into the attracted position.

Breaking and making chemical bonds work the same way. [[red:Separating bonded atoms (breaking a bond) always takes energy in]], just like pulling the magnets apart.

[[green:Atoms coming together and settling into a new bond (making a bond) always releases energy]], just like the magnets clicking together.

theory_blocks.title: Two fixed directions, every single reaction
theory_blocks.body:
In any chemical reaction, two things always happen: some existing bonds in the reactants break, and some new bonds form in the products.

- **Breaking bonds always absorbs energy** (an input), because separating attracted atoms works against the attraction holding them together.
- **Making bonds always releases energy** (an output), because atoms coming together and settling into a stable bond lose energy to the surroundings.

These two directions never swap, in any reaction, exothermic or endothermic. What varies from one reaction to the next is only the *size* of each contribution — how much energy is absorbed breaking the particular bonds involved,

and how much is released forming the particular new bonds.

theory_blocks.title: The balance decides the sign of $\Delta H$
theory_blocks.body:
Since breaking bonds always absorbs energy and making bonds always releases energy, the overall direction of a reaction depends on which contribution is larger.

The two totals are combined into the enthalpy change $\Delta H$ already met in an earlier lesson:

$$\Delta H = (\text{energy absorbed breaking old bonds}) - (\text{energy released forming new bonds}).$$

If $\Delta H$ is negative, more energy is released forming bonds than was absorbed breaking them, so the reaction is **exothermic** overall.

If $\Delta H$ is positive, more energy is absorbed breaking bonds than is released forming them, so the reaction is **endothermic** overall. These are exactly the signs used in an earlier lesson: negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.

This is a qualitative accounting rule here: the figures used are abstract energy 'units' to compare sizes, not specific bond-energy values in kJ/mol.

assets.caption: Breaking the reactants' bonds absorbs 100 units; forming the products' new bonds releases 140 units. $\Delta H = 100-140=-40$ units: negative, so the reaction is exothermic overall.
assets.purpose: Shows the two-stage accounting with 'bonds broken' and 'bonds formed' as separate, comparably scaled bars, and the gap between their tops read as $\Delta H$ (absorbed minus released).

theory_blocks.title: The opposite case, overall endothermic
theory_blocks.body:
The same accounting rule applies whichever way the balance tips. If more energy is needed to break the reactants' bonds than is released forming the products' new bonds,

the reaction is endothermic overall — even though bond making is still, on its own, releasing energy exactly as always.

assets.caption: Breaking the reactants' bonds now absorbs 140 units; forming the products' new bonds releases only 100 units. $\Delta H = 140-100=+40$ units: positive, so the reaction is endothermic overall.
assets.purpose: Mirrors the first figure with the bars swapped, showing that the same two fixed directions (break absorbs, make releases) can give either sign of $\Delta H$.

theory_blocks.title: All the bonds, not just one
theory_blocks.body:
A real reaction usually breaks more than one bond and forms more than one bond. The $\Delta H$ calculation needs the *total* energy absorbed across every bond broken and the *total* energy released across every bond formed — [[red:looking at just one bond's direction,

even correctly, is not enough information to predict the overall outcome]].

keywords.definition: Separating two bonded atoms; always requires an input of energy.
Atoms coming together and forming a new bond; always releases energy.
The total energy absorbed breaking the old bonds minus the total energy released forming the new bonds. A negative value means the reaction is exothermic, a positive value means it is endothermic.

worked_examples.statement: **A simple energy account.** Breaking the bonds in a reaction's reactants absorbs 100 units. Forming the new bonds in its products releases 140 units. Find $\Delta H$ and state the overall direction.
reasoning: $\Delta H$ is the energy absorbed breaking bonds minus the energy released forming bonds, in that order.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta H = 100-140=-40$ units. The negative sign means 40 units are released overall, so the reaction is **exothermic**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both steps individually behave exactly as the rule says — breaking absorbs, making releases — and it is only comparing their sizes that tells you the overall direction.

worked_examples.statement: **The opposite balance.** In a different reaction, breaking the reactants' bonds absorbs 140 units, and forming the products' new bonds releases 100 units. Find $\Delta H$ and state the overall direction.
reasoning: Use the same subtraction in the same order; a positive result means energy was absorbed overall, not released.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta H = 140-100=+40$ units, i.e. 40 units absorbed overall. The reaction is **endothermic** overall.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding this must be exothermic because 'bonds broke and bonds formed, same as before' — the two steps are the same two directions every time, but here breaking needed more energy than making released, giving the opposite overall result.

worked_examples.statement: **Totalling more than one bond.** In a reaction, breaking bond A and bond B together absorbs 180 units in total. Forming new bond C releases 150 units. Find $\Delta H$ and the overall direction, and explain whether this is consistent with the rule that each individual step's direction never changes.
knowns: Total absorbed breaking A and B $=180$ units
reasoning: Add the two breaking contributions first to get the total energy absorbed, then subtract the total energy released to get $\Delta H$.
Check each step still has its fixed direction (breaking absorbs, making releases), independent of the overall result.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta H = 180-150=+30$ units, i.e. 30 units absorbed overall. The reaction is endothermic overall.
worked_examples.interpretation:
This is fully consistent with the rule: breaking (A and B) still absorbed energy, and making (C) still released energy, exactly as always;

it is simply that the breaking total was larger this time, which is what makes the *overall* reaction endothermic.

worked_examples.statement: **Explain the error.** A student writes: 'Breaking bonds releases energy, so every reaction gets some free energy from breaking its reactants' bonds.' Explain what is scientifically wrong with this statement, and state the correct rule.
reasoning: Separate the two claims in the statement: the direction claimed for bond breaking, and the implied overall conclusion.
worked_examples.solution:
The statement has the direction of bond breaking backwards. Breaking a chemical bond always requires an input of energy, not a release, because it means separating atoms that are attracted to each other.

The correct rule is: breaking bonds always absorbs energy, and forming new bonds always releases energy; any 'free' energy a reaction releases overall comes from bond making outweighing bond breaking, never from bond breaking itself.

worked_examples.statement: **A familiar reaction, explained.** Thermal decomposition of a carbonate (heating it strongly so it breaks down into an oxide and carbon dioxide) is known to be endothermic overall: it needs continuous heating to keep going. Using the bond-energy balance for $\Delta H$, explain what this tells you about breaking the carbonate's bonds compared with forming the new bonds in the oxide and in carbon dioxide.
unknowns: What this implies about the two contributions
reasoning: An endothermic overall result means $\Delta H$ is positive: the energy released forming new bonds is smaller than the energy absorbed breaking old bonds.
worked_examples.solution:
Because the reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H$ is positive), the energy needed to break the bonds within the carbonate must be *greater* than the energy released forming the new bonds in the oxide and the carbon dioxide.

Continuous heating is needed because the reaction keeps taking in more energy than it gives back, unlike an exothermic reaction, which can release enough energy to sustain itself.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.

guided_exercises.statement: Breaking the reactants' bonds in a reaction absorbs 95 units. Forming the products' new bonds releases 130 units. Find $\Delta H$ and classify the reaction.
hints: $\Delta H$ is the energy absorbed breaking bonds minus the energy released forming bonds.
A negative value of $\Delta H$ means more was released than absorbed.
Match the sign to exothermic (negative, released overall) or endothermic (positive, absorbed overall).
common_errors: Subtracting in the wrong order (released minus absorbed), which flips the sign of $\Delta H$.

guided_exercises.statement: Breaking the reactants' bonds in a different reaction absorbs 160 units. Forming the products' new bonds releases 110 units. Find $\Delta H$ and classify the reaction, then state whether bond making released energy in this case.
hints: Calculate $\Delta H$ using the same fixed order as before.
A positive value of $\Delta H$ means energy was absorbed overall.
Remember bond making always releases energy on its own, even when the overall reaction is endothermic.
guided_exercises.answer: $\Delta H = 160-110=+50$ units, i.e. 50 units absorbed overall; endothermic. Bond making still released its 110 units as always — it was simply smaller than the 160 units absorbed breaking bonds.
common_errors: Concluding that bond making 'must have absorbed energy' here because the overall reaction is endothermic — bond making always releases energy on its own, regardless of the overall result.

exercises.statement: Breaking the reactants' bonds absorbs 75 units; forming the products' new bonds releases 120 units. Find $\Delta H$ and classify the reaction.
A student states: 'Because breaking the double bond in oxygen releases energy, combustion gets free energy from breaking bonds alone.' Explain the error in this statement.
exercises.answer: Breaking any bond, including a double bond in oxygen, always absorbs energy, never releases it — the statement has the direction backwards. Any energy combustion releases overall comes from the new bonds formed in the products (such as carbon dioxide and water) releasing more energy than was absorbed breaking the original bonds, not from bond breaking itself.
common_errors: Treating bond breaking as a source of released energy rather than an energy cost.

exercises.statement: A reaction breaks one particular bond that, on its own, would absorb 40 units. A student claims this proves the whole reaction must be endothermic. Explain why this claim cannot be justified from the information given, and state what extra information is needed.
exercises.answer: The claim cannot be justified because the overall direction depends on the *total* energy absorbed breaking every bond that breaks and the *total* energy released forming every new bond that forms, not on one bond in isolation. The extra information needed is the energy absorbed breaking every other bond that breaks, and the energy released forming every new bond, so that a complete $\Delta H$ calculation can be done.

exercises.statement: In an industrial reaction, breaking the reactants' bonds absorbs 210 units and forming the products' new bonds releases 165 units. Find $\Delta H$, classify the reaction, and check that the sign agrees with the rule met in an earlier lesson.
exercises.answer: $\Delta H = 210-165=+45$ units, i.e. 45 units absorbed overall; endothermic. A positive $\Delta H$ is exactly an earlier lesson's rule for an endothermic reaction.

exam_questions.statement: In a reaction, breaking the reactants' bonds absorbs 165 units and forming the products' new bonds releases 205 units. (a) Calculate $\Delta H$. (b) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall. (c) Explain why this result does not mean that bond breaking released energy in this reaction.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\Delta H = 165-205=-40$ units. (b) Exothermic. (c) Bond breaking always absorbs energy, in this reaction and every other; the overall exothermic result comes only from bond making (205 units released) outweighing bond breaking (165 units absorbed), not from bond breaking ever releasing energy itself.
mark_scheme: Correct calculation of $\Delta H$: $165-205=-40$ units.
Correctly identified as exothermic overall from the negative sign of $\Delta H$.
States that bond breaking always absorbs energy, with no exception.
Correctly attributes the overall exothermic result to bond making outweighing bond breaking, not to bond breaking itself.

exam_questions.statement: Explain why the statement 'breaking bonds always releases energy' is incorrect, including the correct direction for both breaking and making bonds.
exam_questions.answer: Breaking a bond means separating two atoms that are attracted to each other, which requires an input of energy to overcome that attraction — it always absorbs energy, never releases it. It is forming a new bond, as atoms come together and settle into a stable arrangement, that always releases energy.
mark_scheme: States that breaking bonds always absorbs (takes in) energy.
States that forming bonds always releases energy.
Gives a correct physical reason (overcoming/settling into an attraction) for at least one direction.

mcq.stem: Which statement about breaking a chemical bond is correct?

options.text: Breaking a bond always releases energy.
options.why_wrong: breaking a bond pulls apart two atoms that are attracted to each other, which always costs energy; it is bond making, not breaking, that releases energy.

options.text: Breaking a bond always requires an input of energy.
Breaking a bond releases energy only in exothermic reactions.
options.why_wrong: bond breaking always absorbs energy in every reaction, not only in exothermic ones; whether the overall reaction is exo- or endothermic depends on the balance with bond making.

options.text: Whether breaking a bond absorbs or releases energy depends on the reaction.
options.why_wrong: breaking a bond always requires energy, with no exceptions; it is the overall reaction (the balance of breaking and making) whose classification depends on the specific reaction.

mcq.explanation: Separating two bonded (attracted) atoms always requires energy to overcome that attraction, in every reaction, whether the reaction as a whole is exothermic or endothermic.

mcq.stem: A reaction is endothermic overall. What does this tell you about bond making in this reaction?

options.text: Bond making absorbed more energy than it released.
options.why_wrong: bond making always releases energy, it never absorbs energy; describing it as absorbing more than it released is not possible.

options.text: Bond making did not happen in this reaction.
options.why_wrong: new bonds must form for the reaction’s products to exist at all; bond making still happens, it is just outweighed by bond breaking.

options.text: Bond making still released energy, but less than bond breaking absorbed.
Bond making released energy, and so did bond breaking.
options.why_wrong: bond breaking always absorbs energy, it does not release it; only bond making releases energy here.

mcq.explanation: Bond making always releases energy, with no exception; an endothermic overall result simply means that release was smaller than the energy absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds.

mcq.stem: A reaction breaks bonds X and Y and forms bond Z. Bond X alone would absorb 30 units if considered on its own. Which statement correctly describes how to find the reaction's overall direction?

options.text: Use only bond X's 30 units, since it is the bond that was given.
options.why_wrong: bond Y is also broken and must be included; using only bond X’s value ignores part of the energy absorbed.

options.text: The reaction must be endothermic, since bond X absorbs energy.
options.why_wrong: one bond absorbing energy on its own says nothing about the reaction’s overall direction, which depends on the total absorbed (X and Y) compared with the total released (Z).

options.text: The overall direction cannot be found without knowing exact bond-energy values in kJ/mol.
options.why_wrong: exact values are not needed to state the method, only the totals for bonds broken and bonds formed; the method (compare the two totals) is what decides the direction.

options.text: Compare the total energy absorbed breaking X and Y with the energy released forming Z.

mcq.explanation: The overall direction always needs the total energy absorbed across every bond broken (X and Y here) compared with the total released across every bond formed (Z here); one bond's value alone is not enough information.

mcq.stem: Breaking a reaction's bonds absorbs 85 units; forming its new bonds releases 60 units. What is the reaction's overall classification?

options.text: Endothermic, since $\Delta H = 85-60=+25$ units.
Exothermic, since both breaking and making happened.
options.why_wrong: bond breaking and bond making happen in every reaction; their mere occurrence does not decide the direction, only the sign of $\Delta H$ does, and here $85-60=+25$ is positive.

options.text: Endothermic, since bond breaking always makes a reaction endothermic.
options.why_wrong: bond breaking always absorbs energy, but that alone does not make a reaction endothermic; bond making's release also has to be weighed against it, and only the sign of $\Delta H$ decides.

options.text: Exothermic, since $60-85=-25$ units.
options.why_wrong: $\Delta H$ is the energy absorbed breaking bonds minus the energy released forming bonds ($85-60=+25$), not the other way round; subtracting in the wrong order flips the sign and the classification.

mcq.explanation: $\Delta H$ is energy absorbed minus energy released: $85-60=+25$ units, meaning 25 units absorbed overall, so the reaction is endothermic.

flashcards.front: What direction of energy transfer happens when a chemical bond breaks?
flashcards.back: Energy is always absorbed (taken in) when a bond breaks, with no exception.

flashcards.front: What direction of energy transfer happens when a new chemical bond forms?
flashcards.back: Energy is always released (given out) when a new bond forms, with no exception.

flashcards.front: True or false: breaking a chemical bond always releases energy.
flashcards.back: False. Breaking a bond always absorbs energy; it is forming a new bond that always releases energy.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between bond breaking and bond making, in terms of energy direction?
flashcards.back: Bond breaking always absorbs energy (input). Bond making always releases energy (output). These two directions never swap, in any reaction.

flashcards.front: How do you find whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic from its bond energy changes?
flashcards.back: $\Delta H = $ (total energy absorbed breaking old bonds) $-$ (total energy released forming new bonds). Negative: exothermic. Positive: endothermic.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Breaking any chemical bond always releases energy.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Breaking things apart (snapping a stick, popping a balloon) is often associated with a sudden release of energy in everyday experience, so learners transfer that association to bond breaking.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that bond breaking is exothermic, or that breaking bonds is the step that 'provides' the energy released by an exothermic reaction.
misconceptions.correct_model: Breaking a bond always requires an input of energy, with no exception, because it means pulling two attracted atoms apart against that attraction. This step is always endothermic on its own, regardless of whether the reaction as a whole is exothermic or endothermic.
misconceptions.remediation: Use the magnet analogy: pulling two attracting magnets apart always takes a pull from you (energy in), never the reverse.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Forming a new bond always needs a net input of energy, in the same way breaking one does.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Once learners correctly learn that breaking bonds costs energy, some over-generalise the same direction to bond making instead of learning the opposite rule for it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes bond formation as needing energy, or treats both steps (breaking and making) as if they have the same direction.
misconceptions.correct_model: Forming a new bond always releases energy, with no exception, because attracted atoms moving together and settling into a bond lose energy to the surroundings. This step is always exothermic on its own.
misconceptions.remediation: Use the same magnet analogy the other way: letting two magnets click together releases energy (you can feel or hear the snap), it does not need a pull from you.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The overall direction of a reaction (exothermic or endothermic) can be worked out by looking at just one bond that changes, without considering all the bonds broken and formed.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A single clear example (one bond breaking, one bond forming) is easier to picture than totalling many bonds, so learners generalise from that one case to the whole reaction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts the overall direction from a single named bond change rather than from the total energy absorbed and the total energy released.
misconceptions.correct_model: The overall direction depends on the *total* energy absorbed breaking every bond that breaks, compared with the *total* energy released forming every new bond that forms. One bond's contribution alone is not enough information.
misconceptions.remediation: Give a case where a single bond's direction would suggest one answer, but the full totals give the opposite overall answer, and ask which one is actually correct.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying that breaking a bond releases energy.
common_mistakes.why: Breaking things apart is everyday-associated with a sudden release, which does not match what happens to the bond's own energy.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Use the magnet analogy: pulling attracted magnets apart always takes a pull from you, never the reverse.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying that forming a bond needs an input of energy.
common_mistakes.why: Learners sometimes over-generalise the bond-breaking rule to bond making instead of learning its opposite direction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember forming a bond is always a release, like two magnets clicking together without being pushed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting the overall direction of a reaction from a single bond change.
common_mistakes.why: One clear example is easier to picture than totalling every bond broken and formed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always total every bond broken and every bond formed before comparing the two totals.

common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding that an endothermic reaction means bond making absorbed energy in that reaction.
common_mistakes.why: It is tempting to assume both steps flip direction together with the overall result.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Keep the two fixed directions (breaking absorbs, making releases) separate from the overall result, which only depends on their relative sizes.

exam_notes: State both fixed directions explicitly — breaking always absorbs, making always releases — before giving the overall classification.
Always use the total energy absorbed and the total energy released, naming both numbers, never a single bond's value alone.
Do not introduce specific bond-energy values in kJ/mol unless the question supplies them; at this level the accounting can be done with the units given.
Explicitly state the subtraction for $\Delta H$ (energy absorbed breaking bonds minus energy released forming bonds) before giving the sign and the classification.

summary.big_idea: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy and making bonds always releases energy; whichever of the two totals is larger decides whether the whole reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
key_points: Breaking any chemical bond always requires an input of energy, with no exception.
Forming any new chemical bond always releases energy, with no exception.
$\Delta H = $ energy absorbed breaking bonds $-$ energy released forming bonds.
A negative $\Delta H$ means exothermic overall; a positive $\Delta H$ means endothermic overall.
The overall direction needs the totals across every bond broken and formed, never a single bond's value alone.
formulas: \Delta H = (\text{energy absorbed breaking bonds}) - (\text{energy released forming bonds})
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Breaking always costs energy, making always releases it — only comparing the two totals tells you the reaction's overall direction.

epistemic_overrides.note: Bond energy calculations use average bond energies, which are approximations. Results differ from calorimetric ΔH values. Students should understand this is an estimation method.

summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from chemical energetics accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: Explain the meaning of the terms: (a) endothermic reaction (b) exothermic reaction (c) activation energy.
exercises.answer: (a) Endothermic reaction: a chemical reaction that takes in (absorbs) heat energy from its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls. (b) Exothermic reaction: a chemical reaction that gives out (releases) heat energy to its surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. (c) Activation energy, $E_a$: the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react (it is needed to start breaking the bonds in the reactants).
exercises.full_solution: (a) In an endothermic reaction the products end up with more energy than the reactants started with. The extra energy needed has to come from somewhere, so it is taken from the surrounding air, solution or container, which is why the surroundings feel/measure colder once the reaction has happened. (b) In an exothermic reaction the products end up with less energy than the reactants, because energy has been given out. That released energy heats up the surroundings, so a thermometer placed in the mixture shows a temperature rise. (c) Even an overall exothermic reaction cannot start by itself at room temperature in most cases, because the bonds in the reactants must first be broken, and bond breaking always needs an input of energy. The activation energy is this minimum 'energy hurdle' that colliding particles need in order to react; on an energy level diagram it is drawn as the hump between the reactants' energy level and the peak of the curve, before the pathway drops (or rises) to the level of the products.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Draw energy level diagrams for the reactions given below: (a) $NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)$, $\Delta H = -57$ kJ/mol (b) $2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2H_2(g) + O_2(g)$, $\Delta H = +575$ kJ/mol.
exercises.answer: (a) Because $\Delta H$ is negative, this neutralisation reaction is exothermic, so the diagram has the reactants, $NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq)$, drawn on a higher horizontal energy line on the left, and the products, $NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)$, drawn on a lower horizontal energy line on the right, joined by a curve that dips down from reactants to products; a downward-pointing arrow between the two lines is labelled $\Delta H = -57$ kJ/mol, and the curve still rises slightly just after the reactants' level to show the (small) activation energy before it falls. (b) Because $\Delta H$ is positive, this decomposition of water is endothermic, so the reactants, $2H_2O(l)$, are drawn on a lower horizontal energy line on the left and the products, $2H_2(g) + O_2(g)$, are drawn on a higher horizontal energy line on the right, joined by a curve that rises from reactants to products (with a hump above the products' level for the activation energy); an upward-pointing arrow between the two lines is labelled $\Delta H = +575$ kJ/mol.
exercises.full_solution: Both chemical equations are correctly balanced as printed (checked by counting atoms: in (a), Na, O and Cl each appear once and H appears twice on both sides; in (b), count H and O atoms separately on each side to confirm that their totals match), so the diagrams only need to show the sign of $\Delta H$ correctly. The rule is: if $\Delta H$ is negative, energy has left the system, so the products must be drawn at a LOWER energy level than the reactants (exothermic) — this is the case for (a), the neutralisation of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, which matches the real chemistry fact that neutralisation reactions are exothermic. If $\Delta H$ is positive, energy has been taken in, so the products must be drawn at a HIGHER energy level than the reactants (endothermic) — this is the case for (b), splitting liquid water into hydrogen and oxygen gas, which needs a large energy input (consistent with the fact that forming water from hydrogen and oxygen is strongly exothermic, so the reverse reaction, decomposition, must be strongly endothermic). In both diagrams the x-axis is labelled 'progress of reaction' and the y-axis 'energy/kJ', the two horizontal lines represent reactants and products, the curved arrow connecting them represents the reaction pathway (with a small hump at the start for the activation energy), and a vertical double-headed arrow between the reactant and product lines is labelled with the $\Delta H$ value and its correct sign.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: State which of the following processes is endothermic and which is exothermic: (a) the breaking of a chemical bond (b) the forming of a chemical bond.
exercises.answer: (a) Breaking a chemical bond is endothermic (it requires/absorbs energy). (b) Forming a chemical bond is exothermic (it releases energy).
exercises.full_solution: Bonds hold atoms together because the bonded arrangement has lower energy than the separate atoms; pulling bonded atoms apart therefore means fighting that stabilising attraction, which can only be done by putting energy in — so (a) bond breaking always absorbs energy and is endothermic. The reverse argument applies to (b): when atoms come together and a new bond forms, the atoms move to that lower-energy, more stable arrangement, and the energy difference is released to the surroundings, so bond forming is always exothermic. This is exactly why an overall reaction's $\Delta H$ depends on the balance between the two: if more energy is released forming the new bonds in the products than was needed to break the bonds in the reactants, the overall reaction is exothermic (negative $\Delta H$); if less is released than was needed, the overall reaction is endothermic (positive $\Delta H$).
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: How much energy is released if: (a) 0.5 mole of methane is burned? (b) 5 moles of methane are burned? (c) 4 g of methane are burned?
exercises.full_solution: This question uses the enthalpy of combustion of methane given earlier in the chapter for the reaction $CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)$, $\Delta H = -728$ kJ/mol, meaning 728 kJ of energy are released for every 1 mole of methane burned completely. (a) For 0.5 mol: energy released $= 0.5 \times 728 = 364$ kJ. (b) For 5 mol: energy released $= 5 \times 728 = 3640$ kJ. (c) First convert the mass to moles using the molar mass of methane, $CH_4$: $M = 12 + (4 \times 1) = 16$ g/mol, so moles $= 4 \div 16 = 0.25$ mol; energy released $= 0.25 \times 728 = 182$ kJ. (Note: the question's value of −728 kJ/mol is used because the question is based on it; the accepted data-book value for the enthalpy of combustion of methane is about −890 kJ/mol, but the method is exactly the same.)
